channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: France reports first human Shamonda virus case, says no health risk
item.description: French health authorities said Thursday that the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, had been detected in a human for the first time, in a severely immunocompromised patient who died earlier this month.

item.title: How L-carnitine, found in red meat and exercise supplements, may amplify inflammation
item.description: In a study published Oct. 19 in Cell, Yale researchers identified a previously unknown mechanism by which a nutrient abundant in red meat and commonly used in exercise supplements may amplify inflammation.

item.title: Your brain maps out numbers, including integers and fractions
item.description: From learning to count to solving complex calculations, math requires an inherent organization of information. A team of researchers led by Stanislas Dehaene, Ph.D., and Daniela Valério, Ph.D., at the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit (Unicog) Lab in France took dynamic brain scans of adults presented with fractions and integers. Their findings, published on Oct. 22 in the journal PLOS Biology, revealed a map of brain activity that underlies how we arrange numerical information.

item.title: Mental health support for parents after pediatric intensive care may modestly reduce PTSD and depressive symptoms
item.description: Admission to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) can have lasting psychological effects on both children receiving treatment and their parents. To investigate the effects of psychosocial interventions on parents' emotional health, researchers searched five major academic databases for studies published through January 2026 and analyzed eight randomized controlled trials evaluating psychosocial interventions in parents of children admitted to the PICU. The interventions included visits to follow-up clinics, psychological screening with referral, telephone-based psychoeducation, palliative care consultations and acceptance and commitment therapy delivered via videoconference. The findings are published in the journal Intensive and Critical Care Nursing.

item.title: Comprehensive DNA sequencing reveals hidden drivers of cancer
item.description: Michigan's Oncology Sequencing Program, or MiOncoSeq, was the first of its kind in the nation to sequence patient tumors. Launched in 2010, the program analyzes DNA and RNA from normal tissue and tumors to identify alterations that could help guide treatment.

item.title: Q&A: Expert explains why women should reconsider skipping the Pap smear
item.description: For a long time, the Pap smear has been a lifesaving screening tool for cervical cancer.

item.title: 'Molecular glue' stabilizes protein that inhibits development of non–small cell lung cancer and uterine cancer
item.description: Protein phosphatase 2A plays a central role in controlling many cell signaling pathways, which are frequently disrupted during tumor development and growth.

item.title: Male breast cancer: Risk rises with age, expert explains
item.description: Male breast cancer is far less common than breast cancer in women, but it is usually discovered later: Men with breast cancer often receive the diagnosis after finding a breast lump on their own. Kathryn Ruddy, M.D., an oncologist at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, explains key things to know about male breast cancer.

item.title: MRI scans and DNA data uncover new genetic links to fatty liver disease
item.description: Fatty liver disease is characterized by the accumulation of triglycerides—a type of fat—in the liver. The disease has a strong genetic component, but until now, knowledge about which genes influence its development has been limited. To gain a better understanding, researchers at Karolinska Institutet analyzed genetic data and MRI scans from 71,488 people of European descent in the British UK Biobank database.

item.title: A brain-computer interface may give unresponsive ICU patients a voice
item.description: Unresponsive ICU patients in a new Columbia study were able to raise and lower the frequency of a beeping tone with their minds, via noninvasive EEG electrodes that recorded and translated their brain waves.

item.title: Researchers develop cognitive testing app for at-home use
item.description: The task seems simple on its face: Connect a series of numbered dots scattered on a piece of paper in sequential order. It's the first set of directions participants are asked to follow as part of the Trail Making Test, a neuropsychological assessment designed to measure a person's brain functions, including cognitive flexibility, their capacity to plan and make decisions on the fly, and processing speed.

item.title: Why using AI saves doctors time but won't fix physician burnout
item.description: AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: More than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway's national AI scribe program, about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. Almost 60% report a cut in administrative time.

item.title: Lab study shows needle-free mRNA vaccine protects against COVID and flu
item.description: A needle-free vaccination method protected mice against the viruses that cause COVID-19 and flu, offering a possible new way to deliver mRNA vaccines while limiting unwanted inflammation.

item.title: Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z's weightlifting obsession—here's why
item.description: More than one-quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than vacations or eating out.

item.title: Human neural stem cells found to be susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 variants
item.description: Human neural stem cells that help form the brain and spinal cord are highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2, including omicron variants BA.1 and BA.2, according to new research from the University of California, Riverside. The findings raise concerns about the potential effects of maternal COVID-19 infection on early nervous system development and underscore the importance of monitoring children exposed to the virus before birth.

item.title: GLP‑1 weight‑loss drugs change how people eat, but nausea needs closer study
item.description: Someone taking a weight-loss drug might leave half their dinner because they feel comfortably full. They might also stop because they feel nauseous. Measuring the leftovers would reveal the same result, but tell researchers little about why the person stopped eating.

item.title: 'Average' human genome described for first time, with implications for disease risk
item.description: A new study has characterized the "average" human genome, providing key information on normal human genetic variation and genetic disease risk. The researchers conclude that everyone—regardless of their current health status—could potentially be told they are at risk for numerous conditions based on their genetics alone.

item.title: Scientists reveal how climate studies could predict where and when the risk of Ebola outbreaks increases
item.description: A study led by the University of Malaga has shown that Ebola outbreaks do not occur randomly over time; rather, their occurrence is linked to specific large-scale meteorological patterns, including oscillations in regions thousands of miles away from Central Africa, where an epidemic of this potentially fatal disease is underway.

item.title: Adding emotion management skills to family weight treatment may help teens maintain weight loss
item.description: Researchers from the University of California San Diego have found that adding emotion management skills to family-based behavioral weight management may help adolescents maintain weight loss after treatment ends.

item.title: Excessive weight gain during pregnancy linked to higher risk of severe maternal complications
item.description: A new study of more than 1 million births led by McMaster University researchers has found that gaining too much weight during pregnancy, regardless of a person's starting weight, is linked to a higher risk of life-threatening maternal complications.

item.title: Giving birth again too soon after having a baby could lead to quicker biological aging
item.description: The study of biological aging, how our cells, tissues and organs change over time, independent of how many years have passed, is a growing area of research that aims to help scientists understand the root causes of chronic illnesses and find ways to enhance longevity. A review article published in Trends in Endocrinology & Metabolism discusses the connections between pregnancy and biological aging.

item.title: Study identifies key drivers of microbiome-linked cancer immunotherapy side effect
item.description: Scientists at the University of Pittsburgh uncovered the unstable immune cells that can cause up to 40% of immunotherapy patients to experience serious side effects and showed that diet and microbiome composition influence the side effect's severity.

item.title: Earlier survivorship care linked to lower risk of head and neck cancer recurrence and death
item.description: Beginning survivorship care for head and neck cancer patients earlier is linked to better survival and lower recurrence, according to a new University of Pittsburgh study published in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery.

item.title: Adding a Mirena IUD during surgery can reduce the risk of hysterectomy in women with heavy menstrual bleeding
item.description: Fitting a hormonal intrauterine device (IUD) during surgery to help manage heavy menstrual bleeding reduces a woman's risk of needing a hysterectomy in the following two years by more than half, according to a new open-label randomized controlled trial published in The Lancet.

item.title: Dehydration, UTIs and cognitive health: Getting enough to drink is complicated for people with brain disorders
item.description: For older adults with dementia or Parkinson's disease, staying hydrated can be more complicated than simply drinking more water.

item.title: Clinical trials generate promising results for improving kidney health
item.description: The results of numerous high-impact Phase III clinical trials that could affect kidney-related medical care were presented in person at American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

item.title: How long until wearable brain‑computer interfaces become mainstream?
item.description: Devices that link human minds to computers are progressing rapidly. Already, these brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are allowing patients with severe paralysis to communicate, use digital devices or control smart homes with their brains.

item.title: Drug-free approach shown to reduce depression relapse among new and expectant moms
item.description: A free, online program developed by University of Colorado Boulder researchers has been shown to reduce the risk of depression relapse by double digits among new moms and moms-to-be who have struggled with it before.

item.title: Research finds young adult cancer survivors face gaps in long-term care
item.description: Young adult cancer survivors face gaps in follow-up care caused by factors including geographic mobility and insurance changes, according to an analysis by UTHealth Houston researchers. While most young adults are navigating college, the workforce or relationships, survivors face that and more as they learn to manage their long-term health.

item.title: Hands-on training may help pediatric residents communicate better with families of medically complex children
item.description: New research from Advocate Health's Advocate Aurora Research Institute suggests that giving pediatric residents hands-on training with medical devices may help them communicate more effectively with the families of children frequently hospitalized in pediatric units.
